name: Yew Green
lede: Yew Green is a dull, dark olive green from Robert Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature,” and our archive finds it in paintings six centuries before Ridgway wrote the name down.

sections.title: A tree's name for a drab green
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 dictionary lists Yew Green at hex #556147, grouped with the plant, animal and landscape names rather than the pigment or person names [1]. The Inter-Society Color Council's 1955 catalog of American color names repeats it, filing it in the block it calls grayish olive green [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary is also cited by that 1955 circular as recording the name [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[ivy-green|Ivy Green]], 2.9 units away in color difference and yellower [1]. To the eye it sits closest to the basic term [[hunter-green|Hunter green]], 8.8 units off, with [[old-bamboo|Old Bamboo]] and [[varley-s-green|Varley's Green]] almost indistinguishable neighbors on either side [1]. The yew itself is a dark, dense evergreen, and Ridgway's swatch reads as a greyed-down version of its foliage rather than a bright leaf green [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to this green in 3.35% of 23,781 paintings, 796 of them, as photographed; the stricter within-painting lens counts it in 478 [2]. That makes it more common than 82% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 84 of 1,674 paintings, present in 5.0% of the 1,674 paintings (84 of them) we have from that century, 2.4 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often turns up as a hidden color, in 45% of its 478 appearances, by lightness rank rather than by brand [2]. Henri Rousseau is its most devoted painter here, holding it in 6 of his 13 works, 7.6 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from [2]. The earliest match we have is from 1275, thirty-seven years before Ridgway's earliest dated plate, and 637 years before his 1912 book wrote the name down, a floor rather than a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
